scenario.speaker: marcus
scenario.briefing:
Fielding is done — the survey reached its target of **600 completes**. The closed-ended data is already flowing into the analysis plan, but two questions came back as raw text, and raw text doesn't tabulate: the open-ended **concerns** question and the **"Other, please specify"** on primary use.

That's where coding comes in. **Coding** turns each written answer into exactly one category from a fixed **code list**, so 600 voices become countable data. Dana and I have already built the two code lists from a read of the first hundred responses; your job is to apply them to a batch of responses from each question — 24 concerns, 24 intended uses.

Three rules before you start. **One code per response** — when someone mentions two things, code the theme they lead with or say most forcefully. **Code the topic, not your opinion of it** — "the price is ridiculous" and "it's a bit expensive" both go to the price code, however differently they land. And **respect the Ignore code** — gibberish, blank-adjacent fragments, and answers to some other question get set aside, not force-fitted.

One more thing: on a real team, two coders work the same responses independently and reconcile where they disagree — that's how we know the codes mean the same thing to everyone. Today, I'm your second coder. I've coded both batches already; your codes get checked against mine.

The **Guides** cover the craft. Read the memo I sent you first — it walks through the code lists.

inbox.subject: Field closed at n = 600 — analysis timeline
inbox.body:
It's official: the Neo Smart Living survey closed this morning at exactly **600 completes** — right on the fielding budget the board approved, and the probability plan held up cleanly in the field. Good work on the front end of this study; now we earn our fee on the back end.

Here is the timeline I've committed to Neo:

- **This week:** open-ended coding (you, with Marcus as second coder) and data cleaning.
- **Next week:** tabulation and cross-tabs — barriers, value drivers, concept scores, and price expectations, sliced by the segments Neo cares about.
- **Week after:** the final report and my presentation to Neo's board — positioning, pricing, and the recommendation on the $23,000 question.

Everything downstream depends on the coding being done right. Two questions came back as free text: the **concerns** open-end and the **"Other, please specify"** on primary use. Until those are coded, they're 600 anecdotes; once they're coded, they're evidence — we can say how many respondents raised price versus privacy versus HOA rules, and put those counts next to the closed-ended barrier data.

Marcus has the code lists and your batches ready. Be disciplined about it — the temptation in coding is always to skim. Every response you code becomes a number in my board deck, so read each one like it's the only answer that respondent gave us. Because it is.

— Dana

inbox.subject: How to code open-ends (read before you start)
inbox.body:
Coding is the unglamorous step that makes open-ends usable, so let's do it properly.

**What a code list is.** A short set of categories that covers what respondents actually wrote. Dana and I drafted both lists by reading the first hundred responses, grouping recurring themes, and naming each group. A good list is **mutually exclusive** (a response belongs in one place) and **exhaustive** (every codable response has a home). You'll apply the lists as given — no adding codes mid-stream.

**One response, one code.** Assign the **single most salient theme** — the thing the respondent leads with or states most forcefully. "It's expensive and I'd worry about my HOA" is a judgment call; "It's way too expensive" is not.

**The Ignore discipline.** Some responses can't be coded: keyboard mash, fragments that trail off, or answers to a question we didn't ask. Those get **Ignore** — and using it is a skill, not a failure. Force-fitting garbage into a real code corrupts the counts. But be honest: "No other concerns" is NOT garbage — it's a real answer with its own code. Read the difference.

**Code the topic, not your opinion of it.** "The price is ridiculous" and "cost is a slight concern" both code to price. We're counting themes, not agreeing with them.

**Your second coder.** On a real team two coders code independently, then reconcile disagreements — high agreement (we'd report an intercoder reliability statistic) is what makes the counts trustworthy. I've already coded both batches. Your codes get checked against mine.

— Marcus

pages.intro: Survey question: **"What concerns, if any, would reduce your likelihood of purchasing?"** Assign each response exactly one code from the list. Responses with no codable content get **Ignore**; respondents who state they have no concerns get **No concern stated** — those are different things.

guides.title: Coding open-ended responses
guides.body:
Closed-ended questions arrive as data; open-ended questions arrive as *language*. **Coding** is the bridge: assigning each free-text response to one category from a fixed **code list**, so themes can be counted, cross-tabbed, and compared just like any other variable.

**Building a code list.** Read a healthy slice of the responses (often the first 50–100) before naming anything. Group recurring themes, name each group in plain words, and test the list against fresh responses. Two properties are non-negotiable:

- **Mutually exclusive** — the categories don't overlap, so any response belongs in at most one. If you keep hesitating between two codes, the codes are too close together (or you're not applying the salience rule — see below).
- **Exhaustive** — every codable response has a home. In practice, exhaustiveness is achieved with a small number of substantive codes plus housekeeping codes like "None / no concern" and "Ignore."

Keep the list short. Six to ten codes usually beats twenty: rare themes can share a code, but a splintered list produces counts too small to use.

**The single-most-salient-theme rule.** Real people don't answer in categories; they mention two or three things in one breath. Code the theme the respondent **leads with or states most forcefully** — the thing they'd repeat if you asked, "but mainly?" (Some studies allow multi-coding, but then the counts no longer sum to the number of respondents. This study codes one theme per response.)

**The Ignore code.** Reserved for responses with no codable content: keyboard mash, fragments that trail off mid-thought, and answers to a different question than the one asked. Ignore is a discipline, not a dumping ground — force-fitting an uncodable response into a substantive code corrupts the counts, but exiling a *real* answer to Ignore throws away data. In particular, "I have no concerns" is a substantive, countable answer — it gets its own code, never Ignore.

**Code the topic, not your opinion of it.** The coder's stance, and the respondent's intensity, are irrelevant to code assignment: "the price is ridiculous" and "cost is a slight concern" carry the same code. Intensity can be analyzed separately; the code just says *what the response is about*.

**Intercoder reliability, in one paragraph.** A code only means something if two trained people, working independently, would assign it the same way. Real studies therefore have two (or more) coders code the same responses without conferring, compute an agreement statistic that corrects for lucky matches (percent agreement at minimum; Cohen's kappa or Krippendorff's alpha in published work), reconcile the disagreements, and sharpen the code definitions where the disagreements clustered. Low reliability isn't a coder problem — it's usually a code-list problem, and the fix is better category definitions, not louder insistence.
